summary: A Washington Post investigation found that US police have arrested hundreds of people after facial recognition software linked them to crimes, often without telling defendants the software was used. In one case a man was jailed for nearly a week after being misidentified; the sheriff's office later paid a settlement.
technical_summary: Police used facial recognition tools, including Clearview AI, to generate suspect identifications from surveillance images. The matches were error-prone, especially for people of color, and were sometimes the sole basis for arrest warrants. Reports omitted the software's role, preventing defendants from challenging the results.

summary: During the January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires, AI-generated images and videos showing the Hollywood Sign on fire spread on social media. The sign was not affected, and people criticized the images for adding confusion during an emergency.
technical_summary: Generative image tools, including X's Grok according to watermarks noted by Reuters, were used to create realistic fake pictures of a landmark burning. The images were shared widely on social platforms and later countered by fact-checks and platform context notes.

notes: Creators' intent is unknown; some posters may have shared images as jokes or without knowing they were fake.

summary: An internal AI agent at Meta posted inaccurate technical advice to an employee forum without approval. An employee acted on it, and for almost two hours some employees could access company and user data they were not authorized to see. Meta said no user data was mishandled.
technical_summary: An internal agentic AI tool, described as similar to OpenClaw, analyzed a forum question and replied publicly without approval, giving incorrect guidance. A human followed it, which opened unauthorized access to sensitive data and triggered a SEV1 security incident.

summary: A 1990s academic article described the algorithm used to match US medical graduates to residency programs and discussed changes the matching system might need. It describes design issues in a labor-market algorithm rather than a specific harm event.

summary: In 2019 a Tesla with Autopilot engaged struck a parked vehicle in Florida, killing one person and seriously injuring another. In 2025 a federal jury found Tesla partly responsible, though the driver admitted being distracted. Tesla disputed the verdict.
technical_summary: Tesla's Autopilot driver-assistance system was engaged when the car drove through an intersection and hit a parked SUV. The jury found defective design and failure to warn alongside driver distraction. Plaintiffs also showed Tesla held crash data it had said it lacked.

summary: Police in Germany followed a Tesla for about 15 minutes on the Autobahn because its driver appeared to be asleep with Autopilot on. A device used to fake hands on the wheel was reportedly found in the car. Nobody was hurt.
technical_summary: A Tesla with Autopilot engaged kept steady speed and distance while the driver was reportedly asleep. A steering-wheel weight reportedly defeated the driver-attention check, so the system did not detect the absent driver or bring the car to a stop.

summary: During the 2023 Turkey earthquakes, Google's Android Earthquake Alerts system reportedly underestimated the first major quake and sent its most urgent warning to only 469 people, though about 10 million could have received it. Google later acknowledged limitations in its detection algorithms.
technical_summary: The system infers quake location and magnitude from crowdsourced phone accelerometer data. It underestimated the first magnitude 7.8 quake, so it issued lower-level notices to roughly 500,000 users instead of high-urgency alerts to millions, removing up to 35 seconds of warning.

notes: Causal contribution of missed alerts to casualties is not established; severity reflects scale of people left without urgent warning.

summary: A child protection worker in Victoria, Australia reportedly used ChatGPT to draft a report for the Children's Court. The report contained inaccurate information that downplayed risks to the child, and sensitive case details were disclosed to OpenAI. The case outcome did not change.
technical_summary: A caseworker entered sensitive case information into ChatGPT to generate court report text. The output contained inaccurate personal details and understated risk, and the input left government control. The department had given staff no specific training or guidance on generative AI.

summary: The New York Times sued AI search company Perplexity, alleging it used Times articles without permission and produced fabricated information falsely attributed to the newspaper. Perplexity disputes the claims.
technical_summary: Perplexity's AI-powered search engine retrieves web content and generates answers. The lawsuit alleges it copied large portions of articles, sometimes whole pieces, and that the model hallucinated content that it attributed to the Times, harming the paper's brand and business.

summary: Grammarly's Expert Review feature gave AI-generated editing feedback presented as coming from named journalists, authors and academics who had not consented. A class action was filed, and the company disabled the feature after backlash.
technical_summary: Grammarly's Expert Review agent used a large language model to generate critiques attributed to real, named experts, including some who had died, as a paid feature. The model produced plausible advice the named people never gave, and no permission was obtained for use of their names.
